title: Zero-Amplitude Detection in Centered-Gaussian Quantum States
summary: For centered-Gaussian quantum-state amplitudes at the stated scale, no algorithm faster than order two to the n is known to detect or locate an exact zero, whose use in key recovery remains open.

formal_statement.body: Given a quantum state $\sum_x \alpha_x\lvert x\rangle$ whose amplitudes follow a centered Gaussian distribution, determine whether one coordinate amplitude is exactly zero or no coordinate amplitude is exactly zero, and, when a zero exists, identify its coordinate. When the remaining amplitudes have standard deviation $O(2^{-n/2})$, no algorithm better than $O(2^n)$ is known for this task, and it remains unresolved how to exploit the zero-amplitude property for key-recovery attacks.

scope.domain: This is a quantum-cryptanalysis problem concerning centered-Gaussian quantum states and key recovery.
assumptions: The quantum-state amplitudes follow a centered Gaussian distribution.
For the stated known bound, the remaining amplitudes have standard deviation on the order of two to the minus n over two.
parameters: n: governs the standard-deviation scale and the stated exponential algorithmic bound
scope.unresolved_remainder: Develop an algorithm improving on the stated exponential bound to detect and locate an exact zero amplitude, and determine how to exploit that property in key-recovery attacks.

citations.label: Quantum Linear Key-recovery Attacks Using the QFT

progress.summary: The source presents deciding the zero-amplitude case and identifying its coordinate as an unresolved quantum algorithmic challenge. It reports no algorithm better than order two to the n at the stated scale and no known way to exploit the property for key recovery.
citation_labels: André Schrottenloher et al., Quantum Linear Key-recovery Attacks Using the QFT
